title: On-call VPC firewall runbook sketch and postmortem notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working sketch for an on-call playbook and post-incident notes after multiple customer reports of control-plane reachability failures from on-prem/private VPC deployments. The goal: capture what we observed, immediate mitigations, checks for the next on-call, and a minimal customer-facing firewall rule checklist that SRE/solutions can hand to customers.

Background summary:
- Multiple customers (RWI-2381, RWI-2390) reported that their on-prem nodes suddenly lost reachability to our managed control-plane endpoints (hosted API + deployment control services).
- Symptoms: API requests time out (tcp handshake stalls), SDKs return connection errors, control-plane healthcheck probes failing from customer clusters.
- Affected surfaces: Private (VPC) control plane and some on-prem tunneled deployments using egress proxies.
- Time window: incidents clustered between 2025-01-10 02:12 UTC and 2025-01-10 05:45 UTC.

Quick timeline (UTC):
- 02:07 - Internal alert: Elevated 5xx rate from private control-plane load balancers.
- 02:12 - First customer case opened: long tcp connect times (SDK: ECONNRESET after 30s).
- 02:18 - On-call (Jordan) began triage: confirmed customer traceroutes show RST/ICMP unreachable from last hop.
- 02:35 - Correlated with a routing churn event in cloud region us-east-2 (internal network ops).
- 03:05 - Temporary mitigations applied: route preference change (failover to secondary control-plane subnet) and extended keepalives for active connections. Partial recovery noted.
- 04:20 - Some customers still seeing problems due to customer-side firewall state/conntrack. Worked with one customer to clear conntrack entries; connection recovery confirmed.
- 05:45 - Monitoring trends normalized; tickets transitioned to Solutions Engineering for long-term guidance.

Observed root causes (combined):
- Primary: transient route flapping in provider network caused packets to be blackholed or delayed. Control-plane instances in the primary subnet briefly became unreachable.
- Secondary/Amplifier factors: customer firewall/egress proxies with strict source/destination pinning and short NAT connection timeouts; heavy reliance on sticky NAT meant existing TCP sessions were invalid after failover. Also, some on-prem devices blocked traffic when they saw asymmetric paths (return path via different egress).
- Tertiary: MTU misconfiguration on certain VPN tunnels contributed to TCP stalls for larger TLS handshakes.

Immediate mitigations that helped during incident:
- Rapidly advertised secondary control-plane subnet (internal routing BGP policy) and shifted LB weights to healthy subnets.
- Instructed customers to temporarily allow control-plane IP ranges sourced from confluence:private-deployments/control-plane-ips for both TCP/443 and healthcheck ports.
- For customers behind stateful firewalls/proxies: guidance to clear conntrack and increase NAT timeout for ephemeral ports to at least 300s. Example iptables conntrack clear commands provided below.

Triage checklist for on-call (short):
1. Confirm scope: ping/HTTP probe from multiple regions (use internal synthetic checks) and ask customer for traceroute from affected host.
2. Verify our control-plane LB status: check LB health, instance states, and cloud provider route tables.
3. Check recent routing/BGP changes in region (internal netops notes).
4. If routing flaps seen: failover to secondary control-plane subnet and adjust LB weights.
5. Ask customer to run: traceroute -n <control-plane-ip>, curl -vvv https://<cp-host>/health, and capture tcpdump if possible.
6. For on-prem: check VPN/MTU and conntrack. Provide commands below.

Useful commands: (share with engineers/customers as needed)
- traceroute: traceroute -n -w 1 <control-plane-ip>
- curl debug: curl -v --resolve "api.redwood-controlplane:443:<control-plane-ip>" https://api.redwood-controlplane/health
- tcpdump (on customer host): sudo tcpdump -n -i eth0 host <control-plane-ip> and look for SYN then nothing or SYN,RST
- conntrack flush (linux): sudo conntrack -D -d <control-plane-ip> or to flush by port: sudo conntrack -D -p tcp --dport 443
- iptables NAT timeout hint (conntrack tunables): echo 300 > /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established
- check MTU: ping -c 3 -M do -s 1472 <control-plane-ip> (adjust packet size until success)

Customer firewall rule checklist (minimal, shareable):
- Allow outbound TCP to our control-plane IP set (confluence link) on ports 443 and 6443 (if applicable for k8s control-plane tunnels).
- Allow return traffic and ensure asymmetric routing is tolerated (disable strict reverse path filtering where safe).
- Increase NAT / connection tracking timeouts to >= 300s for established TCP sessions to the control plane IPs.
- If using application proxy, whitelist SNI (api.redwood-controlplane) and allow large TLS handshakes (no aggressive inspection).
- Ensure MTU across VPNs is >= 1400 or enable MSS clamping on the VPN device.

Draft runbook steps (for inclusion in SRE playbooks):
- Detection: Automated alert if >3 customers in region report control-plane timeouts within 30 minutes OR synthetic checks show >5% failed TCP handshakes to control-plane LB.
- Automated first responder: Post to #sre-private-alerts and create an incident ticket with template (region, affected customers, start time, first symptom).
- Triage: follow triage checklist above. If cloud routing event suspected, escalate to NetOps and flip traffic to secondary control-plane subnet.
- Customer remediation guidance: Provide customer checklist and commands; offer remote session to clear conntrack and verify MTU.
- Post-incident: capture packet captures (customer and our LB), store in incident folder, and run regression test (synthetic) for 24h.

Post-incident remediation items (owners & rough ETA):
- NetOps team: improve BGP dampening/monitoring on us-east-2 (owner: Aisha) — ETA 2 weeks.
- SRE: expand synthetic probes to include TCP handshake timings to all control-plane IPs (owner: Jordan) — ETA 1 week.
- Solutions Eng: create customer-facing firewall checklist doc and a short runbook for clearing conntrack on common devices (owner: Maya) — ETA 1 week.
- Engineering (runtime): add graceful reconnect/backoff improvements in SDK to better tolerate asymmetric failover (owner: Tomas) — ETA 3 weeks.

Open questions / items to research:
- Can we provide a small UDP-based lightweight health probe to detect MTU/VPN blackholes faster?
- Should we publish a per-region TTL and update cadence for control-plane IP list to help customers manage iptables rules?
- Investigate whether our TLS handshake size can be reduced for health checks (would reduce MTU sensitivity).

Notes for next on-call:
- If a new incident surfaces, prioritize getting a customer traceroute + tcpdump and a cloud provider route table snapshot within the first 20 minutes.
- Avoid asking customers to change firewall rules unless necessary; prefer transient routing failover first.
- Keep Solutions Eng looped early — they can reduce mean-time-to-repair by coordinating with customer firewall admins.

Appendix: example exchange with a customer (redacted)
Customer: "After your earlier failover things were fine, but they popped again when another network change happened."
SRE: "We saw route flaps in provider BGP — can you please clear conntrack and keep NAT timeouts longer while we stabilise? Also confirm no in-line inspection for TLS flows."
Customer: cleared conntrack with: sudo conntrack -D -p tcp --dport 443 and verified curl now completes.

End of sketch — keep this in engineering/private-deployments as a living doc. Will convert to a formal runbook and a customer one-pager once owners confirm remaining action items.
